extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, judges, and patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria for assessing patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (the Alice two-step framework), especially for software/web-conferencing inventions, and related procedural rules at the motion-to-dismiss stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step test (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-part Alice framework: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); (2) if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether an 'inventive concept' exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Alice/Mayo: Step One asks if claims are directed to an ineligible concept; Step Two searches for an 'inventive concept' that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on claim language but consider specification/prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: The §101 inquiry must focus on the language of the asserted claims themselves, but courts may look to the written description and prosecution history to understand the problem facing the inventor and what the patent describes as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents allow multiple analytical approaches: (1) consult the written description to understand inventor's problem and solution; (2) consider whether any technological improvement is 'embodied in the claims'; (3) analyze whether claims and specification 'describe how the improvement was accomplished.' (Cites: ChargePoint; Visual Memory; Recentive Analytics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific asserted improvement vs. abstract idea (software-specific guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In software cases, the inquiry often turns on whether claims focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities (patent-eligible) or instead on a process/system that qualifies as an abstract idea (patent-ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim language and specification disclose concrete improvements to computer functionality, eligibility is more likely; if they merely implement desired results without technical detail, they are often directed to an abstract idea. (Cites: Int’l Bus. Machs. v. Zillow; Visual Memory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — result-oriented functional claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drafted using largely (if not entirely) result-focused functional language, containing no specificity about how the purported invention achieves those results, are almost always found to be ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented language such as 'able to' or 'arranged to allow' without describing how the results are achieved is a red flag. (Cites: Beteiro; examples in this opinion that claims merely state results for asynchronous review.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Alice Step Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Step Two, claims must include an inventive concept—something more than the application of an abstract idea using well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known to the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept must 'reflect[] something more' than conventional activity. Mere use of conventional components performing their ordinary functions cannot supply the inventive concept. (Cites: Cellspin; Aatrix; Accenture; Affinity Labs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components performing ordinary functions do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification confirms that recited components are conventional and operate according to their ordinary functions (e.g., client applications, data streams, time-scale modification using off-the-shelf algorithms), those components cannot, as a matter of law, constitute an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent itself states conventionality of components or admits similarity to existing components, courts may treat those elements as routine and conventional for Step Two purposes. (Opinion applied this to client applications, data streams, and time-scale modification component.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must show how improvement is achieved to support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed technological improvement must be described in the specification (and, ideally, embodied in the claims) such that a skilled artisan can discern how the improvement is accomplished; mere statements of goals/benefits are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for disclosure of specific means or technical solutions in the specification. Absence of such disclosure supports a finding that claims are directed to an abstract idea. (Cites: Recentive Analytics; Visual Memory; contrasted with Contour IP example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative precedent analysis (distinguish patents that disclose specific means)
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing eligibility, compare to precedent: patents that disclose specific means of achieving an improvement (e.g., generating high- and low-quality streams in parallel) are distinct from patents that merely claim the improvement without concrete implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies to cases like Contour IP (eligible where specific technical means were claimed) vs. Hawk Technology (ineligible where claims recited goals without concrete solutions) to guide analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility can be resolved at Rule 12(b)(6) stage when no factual dispute exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be determined ineligible at the motion to dismiss stage 'when there are no factual allegations that, taken as true, prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ninth Circuit Rule 12(b)(6) standard: accept all factual allegations as true and construe pleadings favorably; Federal Circuit reviews de novo. If the patent/specification themselves demonstrate conventionality or lack of inventive concept, dismissal is appropriate. (Cites: Simio; Aatrix; Bot M8.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Futility standard for denial of leave to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: When a district court denies leave to amend as futile, the futility determination is reviewed de novo; amendment is futile if proposed allegations could not change the §101 analysis given what the patent itself states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent specification confirms conventionality or otherwise forecloses an inventive concept, allowing amendment would be futile and denial is appropriate. (Cites: Mobile Acuity; Sanderling.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court treatment of extraneous materials on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court need not treat a 12(b)(6) motion as one for summary judgment unless it acts to convert the motion by indicating it will not exclude extraneous materials; courts should state when they rely on materials beyond the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court expressly states it did not rely on extra-pleading materials, conversion is not required. (Cites: Swedberg v. Marotzke.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim construction is required before §101 ruling
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is not necessary before deciding §101 unless the patentee proposes a specific claim construction and explains why that construction would change the patent-eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defeat a motion to dismiss based on the need for claim construction, the patentee must propose a specific construction and explain how resolving that dispute would affect the §101 outcome. (Cites: Mobile Acuity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive allegations cannot overcome patent text
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive or contrary allegations in pleadings cannot alter what the patent itself states about conventionality or how components operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent specification explicitly describes components as conventional or describes their operation as similar to existing components, conclusory allegations to the contrary do not change the legal analysis. (Cites: Sanderling Mgmt. Ltd. v. Snap Inc.)
